PC: Request and review patient admission documents, diagnoses, prior treatment, and medications.
May request subsequent vital signs checks.
May request pain management (e.g., Tylenol, Tylenol with a narcotic PO or medication by IV).
Learners should consider obtaining a portable chest x-ray or performing a bedside ultrasound (E-FAST) to diagnose the pneumothorax.
May request additional vascular access and start fluid resuscitation.

Learners may perform a needle and/or tube thoracostomy to treat the pneumothorax which can be performed using a hybrid simulation strategy where a simulated chest model (e.g., TraumaMan) will be positioned at the bedside to allow the participant to continue to interact with the patient while performing the procedure.
MK: Review/analyze initial set of vital signs.
What are the most important things you need to do to get the correct leading diagnosis?
Pneumothorax progressing to tension pneumothorax: (See Appendix L for supporting evidence)

Rib Fracture * Hemothorax * Pulmonary Contusion * Pulmonary Embolism * Syncope related to cardiac arrhythmia (e.g., a fib, Vtach) * Hypovolemia (e.g., dehydration, sepsis) * Anaphylaxis * Stroke/CVA * Pneumothorax * Cardiac Contusion * Splenic or liver laceration/hematoma   (See Appendix L for supporting evidence)
SBP: May request moving crash cart into the room along with continuous 3 - lead ECG monitoring.
May choose to call rapid response or senior resident.
ICS: Communicate with the patient (introduction, diagnostic questions).
Give handoff report to the arriving RRT team member.
